questions.q: What does "collaboration" specifically mean in this guiding principle?
options: Replacing all team-specific tools with a single shared one
Working across organizational boundaries, against the natural pull toward silos
Generic advice to communicate more within your own team
Requiring every team to report to a single manager
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes this principle from vague teamwork advice — it specifically targets the boundaries between teams and functions.

questions.q: Why does a network team hitting its own SLA while a customer-facing incident drags on illustrate a problem this principle addresses?
options: Because SLAs should never be used to measure network teams
Because the customer should have contacted the network team directly
Because this scenario has nothing to do with collaboration or visibility
Because each team optimized its own local metric while nobody owned the end-to-end picture across the boundary
questions.explain: This is the lesson's concrete example of local optimization inside a silo producing a bad outcome overall.

questions.q: Why is "Promote Visibility" treated as a prerequisite for collaboration, not a separate bonus habit?
options: Because visibility tools are required by ITIL 4 licensing terms
Because visibility only matters for public-facing services
Because people collaborating on hidden, outdated, or wrong information will break down even with good intentions
Because collaboration is impossible without a dedicated dashboard product
questions.explain: Without accurate visibility into the actual state of work, collaboration happens on mismatched pictures of reality, which undermines it regardless of intent.

questions.q: What is a concrete symptom, per this lesson, of an organization violating Collaborate and Promote Visibility?
options: The same question getting three different answers in three different meetings because each team works from its own private version of the current state
Every team using exactly the same ticketing tool
A change being reviewed by too many stakeholders
A service desk having a published SLA
questions.explain: This symptom traces back to the same root cause the lesson names: work that should have been visible across a boundary stayed locked inside it.

questions.q: What does "right stakeholders at the right points" mean according to this lesson?
options: Involving every possible stakeholder in every decision, regardless of relevance
Involving only senior leadership in every decision
Notifying stakeholders only after a change has already been deployed
Bringing in people affected by or knowledgeable about the specific work, at the point their input can still change the outcome
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts a security reviewer consulted before deployment (changes the outcome) with one informed afterward (only documents it).
